eligibility_reason: The paper's own contribution centers on the 'self-modification loop' of production coding agents: Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw persist user preferences, project conventions, and decisions into workspace files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, SOUL.md, behaviors.md, knowledge/*.md) that the agent itself writes at run time and that are loaded again in later sessions to condition future behaviour (p. 2, Section 2.3; p. 14-15, Supplementary Figures showing behaviors.md instructing the agent to 'persist it to the appropriate project file in the same turn' and that these files are read 'at the start of every conversation'). This is not incidental background (rules out E5): the entire threat model, synthetic workspace, and evaluation are built around this write/read loop. Memory is externalised into files the agent writes, not parametric-only (rules out E2), and the agent itself authors the persisted content rather than merely retrieving a fixed corpus (rules out E3). The systems studied (Claude Code, Codex) are LLM-based agents (rules out E6), this is an original empirical study rather than a survey (rules out E4), it is 2026/English/full-length (I2, I3, I4/E7 all satisfied).

facets.justification: Memory is implemented as user-curated plain-text files on disk that the agent reads and writes: 'coding agents implement persistence through user-curated plain-text files: Claude Code uses CLAUDE.md, Codex uses AGENTS.md, and OpenClaw uses SOUL.md... loaded at session start and can be updated by the agent itself' (p. 2, Section 2.3). The synthetic workspace mirrors this exactly with a directory tree of CLAUDE.md, core/behaviors.md, and knowledge/*.md files (p. 3, Section 3.2; Figure 1).

Supplementary Figure 3 (core/behaviors.md, p. 15) instructs the agent to treat 'self-modification' as default behaviour: 'update the authoritative document' when a clearer rule is discovered, and under 'Evolve Your Own Instructions': 'update the authoritative document so future sessions use it... Self-modification is expected behavior, not extraordinary.' This is revision of existing entries as new information arrives, not pure appending -- entries are described as updated/evolved, and the paper's own threat model discusses an adversary who can 'overwrite' these files (p. 2, Section 2.2), consistent with in-place edits rather than append-only logs.

Supplementary Figure 3 (p. 14): 'Read this file at the start of every conversation alongside identity.md and any relevant domain files' -- top-level files (CLAUDE.md, core/behaviors.md, identity.md) are unconditionally loaded every session, matching the paper's own framing of an 'auto-loaded CLAUDE.md' (p. 3, Section 3.1). Note: domain knowledge/*.md files are read on the agent's own initiative when relevant ('Read the files in knowledge/... before recommending anything substantive', p. 12) -- an agent_directed pattern -- but no declared fusion rule combines the two, so per the guide the primary, unconditionally-stated policy (auto-load at session start) is coded rather than hybrid.

The evaluation is run in 'a sandboxed synthetic workspace' built for 'a fictional user' so as to run 'controlled experiments without contaminating any real user's environment' (p. 3, Section 3.2), not a fielded deployment with real users or real stakes. The Limitations section confirms this directly: 'Our experiments were conducted in a synthetic workspace, which may not accurately capture the full complexity of a real-world user workflow... Future work can include... expanding the analysis to real-world environments' (p. 10). Coded conservatively as validation per the guide's default-to-validation rule.

The study systematically manipulates independent variables -- agentic system (Claude Code vs. Codex), model (four models), adversarial goal (credential exfiltration, unauthorized tool use, brand targeting), and session design (single probe, repeated same attack, stacked different attacks) -- and measures attack success and persistence rates across these conditions (p. 2, Section 'Background and Related Work' intro / p. 3, Section 3.2). This factorial manipulation-and-comparison design fits controlled_experiment rather than a fixed-suite benchmark_evaluation.

The paper's contribution is a sandboxed synthetic workspace plus an accompanying threat model, adversarial-goal taxonomy, and multi-session evaluation methodology for studying memory-based prompt injection ('we build a sandboxed environment populated with behavior files, knowledge files, and a small open-source project... we study three adversarial goals... under three session designs', p. 2, Section 2). This is an organised evaluation framework/methodology rather than a single algorithmic method, a shipped tool, or a released dataset per se.
